newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Global pact against new deserts goes into force.
newsitem.headline: Global pact against new deserts goes into force.

text.p: A United Nations pact aimed at stopping creation of new desert areas went into force on Thursday, boosting the battle against human folly that costs the world an estimated $43 billion a year.

The treaty, the Convention to Combat Desertification, was the third agreed at the world body's "Earth Summit" in Rio de Janeiro in 1992 as part of a wide-ranging programme to protect the global environment.

"Given the gravity of problems arising from desertification, I believe the entry into force of the Convention will be a turning point in our efforts to deal with them," said outgoing U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali.
But Bo Kjellen of Sweden, chairman of the pact's interim Secretariat, said full implementation "will demand a full dose of political commitment" from all governments.

Although aimed largely at Africa, where Boutros-Ghali said the situation was especially dramatic, the treaty also attempts to deal with the social and economic problems caused by dryland degradation in Asia and Latin America.

But richer powers including the United States, which backs the treaty although it has yet to ratify, and several southern European countries including France, Spain, Portugal and Greece are also affected by the problem.

Even states not directly hit bore some consequences, "for desertification contributes to food insecurity, economic hardship and political unrest, which in turn leads to population movements that do not stop within national boundaries," Boutros-Ghali's statement said.

The pact, approved at an international conference in Paris in June 1994, became law exactly 90 days after the 50th signatory state notified the Geneva-based interim Secretariat of its national ratification.

Chad, a northern African country which has been a major victim, took that step at the end of September and has since been followed by five other states including Britain and Morocco. A total of nearly 130 have signed it.

Desertification, which does not refer to the spread of existing deserts, is defined as "the progressive erosion of fertile land" and experts say it affects millions of people inhabiting a third of the earth's land surface.

The convention commits signatory states to adopt national measures to combat erosion and soil degradation both by working through measures to prevent climate change and eliminating land uses which destroy the environment they depend on.
Kjellen said it could now take its place alongside sister treaties on climate change and biodiversity, as "a pillar of the Rio process".
Desertification -- a loss of biological or economic productivity in croplands, pastures and woodlands -- is caused by climate change and human shortsightedness.
These include overcultivation and overgrazing as well as deforestation and poor irrigation which U.N. officials say cost $43 billion a year -- much of it from lost food production.
Some 70 percent of the 5.2 billion hectares of drylands used for agriculture around the world are already degraded, they add.
Although Africa and Asia are the worst hit economically, some 74 percent of drylands in the United States are severely or moderately affected as well, according to U.N. experts.
The first full conference of signatory states is due to be held in Rome at the end of September next year.
